title: Seven-Layer Dip
subtitle: Refried beans, guacamole, soured cream, salsa, cheese, olives, and jalapeños
excerpt: A party dip built in layers in a dish: refried beans, guacamole, soured cream, salsa, grated cheese, sliced olives, and jalapeños. Served cold with tortilla chips for scooping. A Tex-Mex party staple that takes 15 minutes to assemble.
sourceNotes: Seven-layer dip: a Tex-Mex party dish developed in the American Southwest from the 1970s onwards. The exact origin is debated but the dish became a potluck and party staple across the US from the 1980s. Based on classic American Tex-Mex published sources.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Can be assembled up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerated, covered. Don't add the salsa layer until the last 30 minutes before serving — it can make the soured cream runny if left too long.

content.text: Seven-layer dip is assembled in a wide, shallow dish so all seven layers are visible from the side and every scoop of a chip goes through the whole stack. The layers, from bottom to top: refried beans (spread thickly), guacamole, soured cream, salsa, grated cheese, sliced black olives, and jalapeños. It is served cold, not baked.

items.prepNote: drained and rinsed, mashed with salt and a little olive oil to make refried beans — or use a tin of shop-bought refried beans
mashed with lime juice, red onion, coriander, and salt (see guacamole recipe)
well drained; or use 200g pico de gallo or shop-bought salsa

content.text: Use a clear glass or ceramic dish that holds at least 2 litres so the layers are visible from the sides.
Mash the drained pinto beans with a fork, a glug of olive oil, and generous salt until roughly smooth. Spread in a thick even layer in the base of a wide, shallow dish.
Spread the guacamole over the beans in an even layer, going to the edges. Spread the soured cream over the guacamole. Spread the salsa over the soured cream.
Scatter the grated cheddar evenly across the salsa. Arrange the sliced olives over the cheese. Scatter the jalapeño rings across the top. Add spring onion and coriander if using.
Refrigerate for 30 minutes before serving. Serve cold with tortilla chips.

items.symptom: Layers collapse into each other when scooped
items.cause: Layers too thin or too warm when assembled
items.fix: Make each layer at least 1 cm thick. Chill the assembled dip for at least 30 minutes so the layers firm up and hold their shape when a chip goes in.

items.symptom: Soured cream turns runny after a few hours
items.cause: Salsa layer is too wet and liquid seeps into the cream
items.fix: Drain the salsa very well. Press it through a sieve or use pico de gallo with most of the liquid drained off. Don't add the salsa layer until the last 30 minutes before serving if making ahead.

items.symptom: Guacamole goes brown through the layers
items.fix: Spread the soured cream immediately over the guacamole so no air touches it. The surrounding layers protect the guacamole from oxidising.

items.cause: Dish too deep and narrow, so chips can't reach the bottom layers
items.fix: Use the widest, shallowest dish you have. A 30 cm diameter shallow bowl or serving dish gives a better ratio of bottom-layer-to-top-layer than a deep bowl.

content.text: Seven-layer dip became a US party staple in the 1980s as a way to serve all the Tex-Mex condiments in one dish for a crowd. The number of layers varies; five, six, seven, and eight are all common. The layering order matters. Beans go at the bottom (stable and dense), perishable toppings on top (cheese, jalapeños, olives), and temperature-sensitive layers (guacamole, soured cream) sandwiched in between. The surrounding layers protect the guacamole and soured cream from air and heat.
